item.title: OpenAI Will Only Sell GPT-5.6 Sol to Trump-Approved Customers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI is restricting its new GPT-5.6 Sol model to buyers vetted by the Trump administration, as Washington's cybersecurity review of frontier AI hardens into a gatekeeping regime.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI said Friday that its newest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, will be available only to customers the Trump administration approves. Read that again. A private frontier lab is letting the federal government decide who is allowed to buy its product. That arrangement did not exist a year ago.

OpenAI is not alone in it. Anthropic said roughly the same week that the administration had cleared a limited release of its strongest cybersecurity model, two weeks after the Commerce Department effectively banned it outright. Both of the country's leading labs are now shipping their best models through the same government turnstile.

The stated reason is cyber capability. Officials grew alarmed after Anthropic warned earlier this year that its Mythos model was good enough at finding software flaws that it could be turned into a weapon against critical networks. Once a vendor says the quiet part out loud, the regulators have to act on it, and a vetting process for who gets access to the most capable models is what that action looks like.

Strip away the security framing and this is industrial policy. Approval lists are how governments pick winners and losers, and a model rationed by federal sign-off is a strange thing to put in an S-1. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have been circling public offerings, and explaining to investors that your flagship product ships only to a government-approved customer roster is not the growth story either of them wanted to tell.

The harder problem is that controls only bite if the capability is scarce. China's GLM-5.2 has been measured matching Anthropic on cybersecurity tasks, and it ships as open weights anyone can download. Watch two things from here: who actually lands on the approved list, and whether an open-weight model that nobody controls makes the whole regime academic.

item.title: Onsemi's $7 Billion Synaptics Deal Is a Bet on Edge AI Silicon
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Onsemi is buying Synaptics in an all-stock deal worth about $7 billion, its largest ever, to push deeper into edge AI, robotics, and connected-device chips.
item.content:encoded:
Onsemi agreed on June 25 to buy Synaptics in an all-stock transaction worth roughly $7 billion, the biggest acquisition in the chipmaker's history. The terms set a fixed exchange ratio of 1.35 onsemi shares for each Synaptics share, about a 19% premium on the recent average price.

The fit is more logical than most chip mergers. Onsemi's strength is power, analog, and sensing silicon. Synaptics brings touch, audio, wireless connectivity, and a line of low-power edge AI processors. Bolt them together and onsemi gets a fuller stack for what it's calling physical AI, the chips that let robots, vehicles, and connected devices sense and act without phoning home to a data center.

Onsemi says the deal widens the markets it can chase by $30 billion, to a total addressable $243 billion by 2030, with $200 million in annual synergies inside 18 months of closing. Those are the buyer's own projections, and the gap between a slide-deck total addressable market and actual revenue is where a lot of semiconductor acquisitions quietly underperform.

Paying entirely in stock keeps cash on the balance sheet but dilutes existing onsemi holders, a tell that management would rather conserve money than spend it at this point in the cycle. The deal is expected to close in mid-2027, and large cross-border chip mergers now move through a gauntlet of regulators, China's included, that can stretch timelines and attach conditions.

Edge AI has been the promised next leg of growth for the analog and sensing vendors for a while. Onsemi just made its largest bet that this is the year it starts paying.

item.title: Rocket Lab Buys Iridium for $8 Billion to Take On Starlink
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Rocket Lab is acquiring Iridium's 66-satellite network, licensed L-band spectrum, and 2.55 million subscribers in an $8 billion cash-and-stock deal to become a full-stack space company.
item.content:encoded:
Rocket Lab spent years as the company that builds rockets and small satellites for other people. As of June 29, it wants to own the constellation too. Rocket Lab agreed to acquire Iridium Communications for about $8 billion, paying $54 per share split evenly between cash and Rocket Lab stock, a roughly 24% premium to where Iridium last traded.

What Rocket Lab is actually buying is operational. Iridium runs a 66-satellite low-Earth-orbit network that already works, plus globally licensed L-band spectrum and a subscriber base north of 2.55 million across government, defense, aviation, and maritime customers. Spectrum that's already licensed worldwide is close to impossible to assemble from scratch, and that, more than the hardware, is the prize.

The pitch is vertical integration: one company that designs, builds, launches, and operates its own constellations instead of stitching that chain together across vendors. It puts Rocket Lab in more direct competition with SpaceX and Starlink, and the L-band angle also feeds the growing defense appetite for positioning and timing that doesn't depend on GPS.

The skeptical read is worth holding onto. Rocket Lab is very good at launch and at manufacturing small satellites. It has never run a global subscription communications network with millions of paying customers, and operating one is a different muscle than building the parts. Integrating Iridium's network, its 500-plus partners, and its billing relationships is where deals like this tend to get hard.

The transaction is expected to close in mid-2027, pending Iridium shareholder and regulatory approval. That's a long runway, and a lot can shift in the satellite market before the ink dries.

item.title: DirtyClone Hands Any Local User Root on Unpatched Linux Boxes
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: JFrog published a working exploit for CVE-2026-43503, a Linux kernel flaw that turns an unprivileged shell into root by abusing how the network stack clones packets.
item.content:encoded:
JFrog Security Research published the full exploit chain for CVE-2026-43503 on June 25, and the part that matters is that it works. Any unprivileged local user can ride this flaw straight to root. The researchers named it DirtyClone, and it's the latest member of a kernel bug family that keeps producing variants.

The technique is the same one that powered DirtyFrag and Fragnesia before it: trick the kernel into treating read-only, file-backed page-cache memory as if it were a writable network buffer. The bug lives in how socket buffers reference shared page-cache memory, and it gets weaponized through in-place cryptographic transforms in subsystems like XFRM/IPsec or RxRPC. Different packet path, same root cause.

Here's the uncomfortable part. The fix has been in the Linux mainline since May 21, but a mainline patch does you no good until your distribution ships it, and many haven't. Debian and Fedora are vulnerable in their default configurations because they enable unprivileged user namespaces. Ubuntu 24.04 and later have partial AppArmor mitigations and are still listed as affected.

Local privilege escalation sounds less scary than remote code execution until you remember where Linux actually runs. Multi-tenant servers, Kubernetes nodes, CI/CD runners, container hosts. In all of those, an attacker who already has an unprivileged foothold and a reliable path to root has effectively won. A public, working PoC just handed them the second half.

There's a one-line mitigation while you wait for your distro: set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0, which cuts off this entire family's escalation path. That it keeps working as the fix for variant after variant raises a fair question about whether unprivileged user namespaces are worth leaving on by default at all.

Patch when your distribution ships the update. Until then, turn the namespaces off where you can.

item.title: Oracle E-Business Suite Flaw Is Under Attack a Month After the Fix
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-46817, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in Oracle Payments, to take over E-Business Suite instances that never applied May's patch.
item.content:encoded:
The first sign someone was using the new Oracle bug came from a honeypot. Over the weekend of June 27, Defused Cyber watched an attacker exploit CVE-2026-46817 against its E-Business Suite decoys, the first confirmed in-the-wild use of a flaw Oracle had already patched.

The vulnerability sits in the File Transmission component of Oracle Payments. It scores a 9.8, and the reason it's that high is simple: an unauthenticated attacker with nothing more than HTTP access can take over a vulnerable instance through a low-complexity attack. No credentials, no user interaction. It affects Oracle Payments versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15.

Oracle shipped the fix in its May Critical Security Patch Update, released May 28. That means the patch has been sitting available for a month while exploitation only kicked off now. The window between a vendor disclosing a flaw and attackers operationalizing it keeps shrinking, but the window between disclosure and customers actually patching never seems to.

E-Business Suite is the kind of target that rewards patience. It's the ERP backbone for finance, procurement, and payments at a lot of large organizations, which means it holds exactly the data that makes extortion pay. Anyone who watched the mass E-Business Suite campaign tear through unpatched instances last year already knows how this movie ends if the patch doesn't get applied.

There's no public proof-of-concept yet and no prior exploitation history, so the people hitting this had to find the path themselves, which usually signals a more capable operator rather than a spray-and-pray crowd. If you run E-Business Suite, the May CSPU is not optional anymore. Apply it, then check your Payments module exposure and your logs for unexpected File Transmission activity.

item.title: SimpleHelp's CVSS 10 Auth Bypass Is Dropping Djinn Stealer
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added the SimpleHelp OIDC authentication bypass to its exploited list after attackers used it to forge technician sessions and deploy a cross-platform infostealer.
item.content:encoded:
The remote-support software that IT teams install to log into other people's machines is now the way in. CISA added CVE-2026-48558, an authentication bypass in SimpleHelp, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 29 after researchers caught it being used to push malware through internet-facing servers. It carries a CVSS score of 10. There is no higher number.

The flaw lives in SimpleHelp's OpenID Connect login flow. When OIDC is configured, the server accepts identity tokens without verifying their cryptographic signature. So an unauthenticated attacker can forge a token, stuff it with whatever identity claims they want, and walk away with a fully authenticated technician session. From there they control the remote-support server and everything it can reach.

Horizon3.ai disclosed the bug publicly on June 12, two-plus weeks before CISA confirmed real-world abuse. By the time it landed on the KEV list, attackers were already using it to plant a two-stage payload.

Stage one is a loader the researchers call TaskWeaver, delivered as a heavily obfuscated single-line Node.js file masquerading as jquery.js. It fingerprints the host, embeds an RSA public key, and pulls down a payload tailored to what it finds. Stage two is Djinn Stealer, which reuses the same obfuscation framework and the identical RSA key. Djinn runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and it goes after credentials from cloud consoles, source control, package registries, AI coding assistants, browsers, SSH keys, and crypto wallets.

Remote management and monitoring tools keep ending up at the center of these incidents for a reason. They run with high privilege, they're exposed to the internet by design, and defenders treat their traffic as trusted. SimpleHelp has been here before, with a separate set of flaws that drew CISA attention in 2025. The vendor patches, the install base lags, and attackers walk through the gap.

Federal agencies have 14 days to remediate under Binding Operational Directive 22-01. Everyone else should patch now and not wait on the clock. If your SimpleHelp box was internet-facing with OIDC enabled, assume a session could have been forged already: rotate technician credentials, pull the logs, and hunt for jquery.js and stray node.exe activity before you call it clean.

item.title: Mistral's OCR 4 Bets Document Extraction Is a Product, Not a Model
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Mistral shipped OCR 4 as a managed enterprise service with per-page pricing, a notable turn for a company best known for open weights.
item.content:encoded:
Mistral built its reputation handing out open-weight models. OCR 4, its new document extraction release, goes the other way. It's a commercial product with per-page pricing, sold as a managed service rather than a checkpoint you download and run yourself.

The pitch is structure, not just text. OCR 4 returns bounding boxes, per-element confidence scores, and block classification that separates a table from a heading from a paragraph, and it's offered both through an API and as a self-hosted deployment for companies that can't send sensitive documents to someone else's cloud. That second option is the concession to the open-weight crowd Mistral grew up with.

It's worth being clear-eyed about what this is. Pulling characters off a page is close to solved; the hard, unglamorous work is producing structured output reliable enough that a human doesn't have to recheck every field. Confidence scores are Mistral's answer to that, and they're the feature to scrutinize, because the review burden is what kills most document-AI projects before they pay for themselves.

The interesting tension is strategic. Mistral is now playing both sides of the document-AI split: open weights for teams that want to self-host and parse on their own terms, and a managed, metered product for teams that want a vendor to own the accuracy. Whether enterprises pay per page for that, or push the open option until the bills get uncomfortable, is the question OCR 4 is really testing.

item.title: Nvidia's RTX Spark Brings a Grace-Blackwell Superchip to Windows PCs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Nvidia's RTX Spark pairs a 20-core Grace CPU with a Blackwell RTX GPU for a petaflop of local AI, and it ships this fall in machines from Dell, HP, Lenovo and Microsoft.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia spent years selling the chips that train AI in data centers. At GTC Taipei on June 1 it revealed the part meant to run AI on your desk. RTX Spark packages a 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, co-designed with MediaTek, alongside a Blackwell RTX GPU, the two linked over NVLink-C2C in a single module.

The specs are aimed squarely at local inference. Nvidia quotes one petaflop of AI performance, up to 128GB of unified memory, and enough headroom to run a 120-billion-parameter model with a one-million-token context window without leaving the machine. The GPU side carries 6,144 CUDA cores and fifth-generation Tensor Cores with FP4 precision.

What makes this more than a spec sheet is whose turf it's on. RTX Spark is Nvidia stepping down into the PC processor market that Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have split among themselves. The market noticed immediately; shares of all three slipped after the unveiling. Nvidia owning the GPU was old news. Nvidia owning the whole system-on-chip in a consumer laptop is the shift.

The honest caveat is that none of this is buyable yet. RTX Spark is slated for fall in PCs from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface, and MSI, with Acer and Gigabyte to follow. Until those ship and someone runs a 120B model on a laptop on battery, the petaflop is a keynote number. Worth watching, not yet worth believing.

item.title: Device Code Phishing Went From Spy Tool to Off-the-Shelf Kit
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A technique that was Russian-state tradecraft 18 months ago now ships in commodity phishing kits, and detections have climbed sharply through 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Huntress logged a roughly 14-fold jump in device code phishing over the first four months of 2026 compared with the back half of 2025. Six months in, researchers are tracking around 18 distinct kits in circulation and a 37x rise in detections. The technique used to be associated with a handful of Russian-linked espionage campaigns. Now anyone with a subscription can run it.

The appeal is that it sidesteps the things defenders rely on. In a device code flow, the attacker kicks off a legitimate OAuth login on the real vendor's site, then sends the target a genuine login page and a short code to enter. The victim authenticates on the actual service, against actual MFA, and approves the code. The attacker walks away with the session tokens. There's no fake domain to flag and no password to capture, which is exactly why it slides past defenses tuned for those signals.

The shift to commodity is the real story. Tycoon2FA, an established adversary-in-the-middle kit, added device code phishing to its menu, and its operator started selling the capability as a service after an infrastructure disruption in February. Kits like EvilTokens, Kali365, Ghost Hub, and Cyb3r are now doing the heavy lifting on landing pages. Crews that were running AiTM phishing are pivoting wholesale.

Because the prize is a stolen token rather than a stolen password, a password reset does nothing to evict the attacker. The defenses that bite are conditional access policies that block or constrain the device code grant, phishing-resistant FIDO2 keys, and alerting on token issuance from unexpected locations. If your identity provider lets you disable the device code flow for users who don't need it, that's the cheapest win on the board.

item.title: Microsoft Threatens a Researcher Over Two Unpatched Defender Bugs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: RedSun and UnDefend turn Windows Defender into a path to SYSTEM and still have no fix, while the researcher who disclosed them says Microsoft threatened them instead of patching.
item.content:encoded:
Three local privilege escalation techniques have a common ingredient: Windows Defender itself. They're named BlueHammer, RedSun, and UnDefend, and the unifying trick is abusing Defender's own privileged file operations to climb from a normal user to SYSTEM. The security tool becomes the way in.

Microsoft already shipped a fix for one of them. BlueHammer, tracked as CVE-2026-33825, is a time-of-check to time-of-use race in Defender's remediation engine; it was patched in April Patch Tuesday. From SYSTEM, the same exploit chain can dump and decrypt the SAM database and reset local passwords. The other two are the problem. RedSun abuses Defender's cloud file rollback, which restores a flagged file without validating where it writes, letting an attacker redirect that write into a privileged directory. UnDefend quietly degrades Defender's update mechanism so the gap stays open. Both are still unpatched, and Huntress says all three have been used in real attacks, with intrusions starting from stolen VPN credentials.

Here's the ugly part. The three exploits were published as working proof-of-concept code by an anonymous researcher using the handles Chaotic Eclipse and Nightmare Eclipse, explicitly as a protest. Their account is that Microsoft's Security Response Center mishandled the reports, threatened them, and disabled their accounts rather than coordinating a fix. Microsoft hasn't disputed the threat allegation in public.

Drop the question of who behaved worse and the operational picture is bad either way. Two flaws that hand attackers SYSTEM on fully updated Windows 10, 11, and Server are sitting in the open with public exploit code and no patch. The dispute that produced that situation is exactly the kind of standoff coordinated disclosure exists to prevent.

Until fixes land, treat Defender's privileged operations as attack surface rather than a backstop. Restrict who can manipulate quarantine and rollback paths, watch for binaries appearing in user directories, and alert on tunneling tools beaconing out. A vendor that answers a bug report with a lawyer instead of a patch teaches the next researcher to skip the report and go straight to publishing. That lesson costs everyone.

item.title: KDDI Breach Puts Up to 14.2 Million ISP Email Logins at Risk
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A flaw in third-party software inside KDDI's shared email platform exposed addresses and passwords for as many as 14.2 million accounts across six Japanese ISPs.
item.content:encoded:
Fourteen point two million email logins. That's the ceiling on what a single intrusion at Japanese telecom KDDI may have exposed, and the reason it reached so far is the part worth sitting with: most of those accounts don't carry the KDDI name.

KDDI says it detected unauthorized access on June 17 in an email system it operates on behalf of other providers. Both addresses and passwords are in scope. The affected brands span six internet service providers riding on that one backend: STNet, KDDI Web Communications, JCOM, Chubu Telecommunications, Nifty, and Biglobe. A customer of any of them could be exposed without ever having signed up with KDDI directly.

The root cause, per KDDI, was a vulnerability in third-party software used in the email platform. The company hasn't named the product. What the incident really illustrates is consolidation risk. When six consumer ISPs share one mail backend, a single bug in one dependency becomes a breach across all six brands at once. That's efficient until the day it isn't.

KDDI says it has modified the affected system, is working with the impacted ISPs to notify users, and is cooperating with Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. The 14.2 million figure is an upper bound on accounts that could be affected, not a confirmed count of compromised credentials. The investigation is ongoing.

If you hold mail at any of those six providers, change the password now and change it anywhere you reused it. Email passwords are reset-everything passwords. Whoever has them can pivot into every account that uses that address for recovery, which is the real reason a mail breach is worse than the headline number suggests.

item.title: The 'Tokenmaxxing' Era Is Ending as Companies Rein In AI Bills
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Enterprises that told staff to burn as many tokens as possible are now demanding ROI, and some are routing traffic to cheaper models.
item.content:encoded:
Uber went through its entire annual AI budget in four months. The company's CTO, Praveen Neppalli Naga, told The Information as much earlier this year, and the response was the tell: Uber put spending tiers on some AI tools, starting at a $1,500-per-month base, with employees having to request anything above that. When a company that size starts metering token use like an overage plan, the mood has shifted.

The thing that's ending has a name. "Tokenmaxxing" was the brief period where employers told developers to use as much AI as humanly possible and treated raw token consumption as a stand-in for productivity. More tokens meant more innovation, supposedly. For a year that logic held, because the spending was a land grab and nobody wanted to be the team that under-invested.

Now the same leaders want receipts. Tighter controls, clearer return on investment, and cheaper alternatives where the expensive model isn't earning its keep. The most pointed example: the CEO of the AI startup Lindy moved all of his company's traffic off Anthropic's Claude and onto DeepSeek, the cheaper Chinese open-weight option, and watched the cost curve fall off a cliff. That's not a rounding-error saving. That's a different bill.

The timing is awkward for the two biggest labs. OpenAI and Anthropic both filed confidentially for what could be historic IPOs in early June, right as their largest enterprise customers start asking why the monthly invoice keeps climbing. Models like Zhipu's GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek give those customers a credible threat to walk, and a credible threat is all you need to renegotiate.

None of this means demand for AI is shrinking. It means the era of unmetered, ROI-optional spending is over, and the providers that win the next phase will be the ones whose pricing survives a CFO actually reading the line items.

item.title: Zhipu's GLM-5.2 Is the First Open-Weight Model That Feels Frontier
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: China's Zhipu shipped MIT-licensed weights that land within a point of Claude Opus on an agentic benchmark at roughly a fifth of the price.
item.content:encoded:
For two years the open-weight crowd has had to settle for "good enough." GLM-5.2, from the Chinese lab Zhipu, is the model that stops the apologizing. Released under a full MIT license on June 17, it scores within about a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on a widely cited agentic benchmark, and it does it at roughly a fifth of the cost. Practitioners who've actually run it, not just read the chart, keep describing it the same way: the first open model that feels plausibly frontier in daily use.

The numbers behind that have texture. It's a mixture-of-experts model, 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active per token, and the context window has been stretched to one million tokens. On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, GLM-5.2 lands at 51, ahead of MiniMax-M3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro at 44 and Kimi K2.6 at 43. That ordering matters less than the gap it closes: the best open model is now trading blows with the closed ones rather than chasing them by a generation.

The price is the headline for anyone running real workloads. Through a host like OpenRouter, GLM-5.2 runs around $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output. GPT-5.5 sits at roughly $5 and $30. Claude Opus is near $5 and $25. When a model is one-fifth the cost and a rounding error behind on quality, the math starts making the decision for you.

There's a real distinction worth keeping straight, though. Open weights mean you can download GLM-5.2 and run it on your own hardware, where your data never leaves your network. Calling Zhipu's hosted API is a different deal, and sending sensitive prompts to a Chinese-operated endpoint carries the data-governance questions you'd expect. The benchmark wins are also benchmark wins. A score of 51 doesn't tell you how it handles your codebase or your weird internal tooling, and the only way to know is to try it.

The timing stings for the US labs. CNBC framed it bluntly this week: Zhipu is closing in while OpenAI and Anthropic are partly held back by Washington's release controls. A capable model you can host yourself, license freely, and run cheap is exactly the thing that erodes a premium API's pricing power. That pressure is already showing up in how companies budget for AI.

item.title: Google Patches Its Fifth Chrome Zero-Day of 2026, Already Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-11645 is an out-of-bounds memory bug in Chrome's V8 engine that attackers were exploiting before the fix shipped.
item.content:encoded:
Five. That's how many actively exploited Chrome zero-days Google has patched since January, and the count is only half the year. The latest is CVE-2026-11645, an out-of-bounds memory access in V8, the JavaScript and WebAssembly engine that does the heavy lifting on every page you open. Google says plainly that it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-11645 exists in the wild."

An out-of-bounds bug in V8 is the kind attackers like because it's reachable from a web page. A crafted site corrupts memory inside the engine and, chained with the right follow-on, becomes code running in the browser's context. The flaw is rated high severity, with a CVSS of 8.8 in the public scoring. The fix lands in Chrome 149.0.7827.102 for Windows and Linux and 149.0.7827.103 for Mac.

An anonymous researcher reported the bug to Google a couple of weeks before the patch shipped, reportedly earning a five-figure bounty. The faster turnaround between a private report and an in-the-wild exploit is becoming the pattern, and it isn't an accident. Google and Microsoft have both pointed to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a reason patch volumes keep climbing. Microsoft's June update alone topped 200 CVEs. More eyes, human and machine, on the same memory-safety bugs means more of them surface at once.

This isn't a Chrome-only problem either. Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi all ride on Chromium and inherit V8, so they're exposed until each ships the same fix. If you maintain any of those in a fleet, they're on your list too.

Updating takes ten seconds and most people skip it anyway. Open the menu, go to Help, click About Google Chrome, and let it pull the update, then hit Relaunch. The fix does nothing sitting in a tab you never restarted.

item.title: ShinyHunters Hit 100+ PeopleSoft Servers Through an Oracle Zero-Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-35273 let attackers run code on PeopleSoft with no login, and Mandiant says two-thirds of the affected organizations are universities.
item.content:encoded:
The calling card was a file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT, dropped into PeopleSoft directories after the attackers had already taken what they came for. The crew behind it is ShinyHunters, and the way in was CVE-2026-35273, a remote code execution flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools rated 9.8 out of 10. No login required, no user interaction, just network access over HTTP to a vulnerable instance.

The bug lives in the Updates Environment Management component, the piece behind the Environment Management Hub known as PSEMHUB. Mandiant dated the activity to a window between May 27 and June 9. Oracle didn't publish its out-of-band advisory until June 10, which means it was a true zero-day the entire time attackers were working through it.

Mandiant, now part of Google, notified more than 100 organizations whose internet-facing endpoints matched the vulnerable fingerprint. Roughly 68 percent of them are in higher education, most in the United States. Some blocked the activity in time. Others were compromised and watched their data land on the ShinyHunters leak site, with the University of Nottingham among the first confirmed victims.

The post-exploitation work was unglamorous and effective. After landing on a PeopleSoft host, the attackers sprayed a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords over SSH to reach other internal machines, compressed stolen data with zstd, and shipped it out over an SSH connection to the server hosting a public mirror of their leak site. Nothing here is exotic. It's a known group running a clean playbook against a class of systems that universities and large enterprises run wide open for staff and student self-service.

If you run PeopleSoft, the PeopleTools patch from Oracle's June 10 alert is the floor, not the ceiling. Assume anything reachable before you patched may already be compromised, hunt for that marker file and unexpected SSH activity between PeopleSoft hosts, and reset the credentials that were sitting on those servers. The leak-site postings are still trickling out, so the list of named victims isn't final.

item.title: Self-Spreading Miasma Worm Poisons 20+ npm Packages in Seconds
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A hijacked maintainer account pushed credential-stealing updates to Leo Platform and RStreams packages, and the malware republishes itself to spread.
item.content:encoded:
The whole thing took under three seconds. Late on June 24, an attacker who had taken over the npm maintainer account "czirker" pushed poisoned updates to more than 20 packages used by the Leo Platform and RStreams data-streaming projects. There was no human at the keyboard timing it. The publish run was fully automated, which is how you compromise two dozen package versions faster than most people can read a single changelog.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence flagged the campaign, with extra technical analysis from Sonatype. The malware family is called Miasma, and it does two things well. First, it hunts for secrets: AWS, Azure and GCP credentials, GitHub tokens, Kubernetes secrets, HashiCorp Vault access, 1Password data, and the victim's own npm publishing tokens. Second, and this is the part that makes it dangerous, it uses those stolen npm tokens to republish itself into more packages. It's a worm. Steal a maintainer's keys, ship a tainted version under their name, harvest the next maintainer's keys, repeat.

If that pattern sounds familiar, it should. Miasma is the same lineage as the Shai-Hulud self-propagating npm attacks, and a "mini Shai-Hulud" toolkit went public on GitHub earlier this month, lowering the bar for anyone who wants to run this play. Miasma also showed up at the start of June in the @redhat-cloud-services compromise, where a hijacked Red Hat employee GitHub account was used to push malicious orphan commits into RedHatInsights repositories, poisoning around 32 packages that pulled roughly 80,000 weekly downloads between them.

The uncomfortable detail in the Red Hat case was that the malicious commits bypassed code review entirely. The June 24 round skips review too, because once an attacker holds a publishing token, npm just accepts the upload. Two-factor authentication on the human login doesn't help when the token is what's being abused.

For anyone shipping software, the move is the boring one that works: pin dependencies to known-good versions, turn on npm's granular access tokens with the shortest viable lifetime, and audit your lockfile for any package that updated in the last few days across the Leo Platform or RStreams trees. If a build pulled a poisoned version, treat every credential that touched that build host as burned and rotate it. The worm's entire business model is the credentials you didn't rotate fast enough.

item.title: CISA Adds PTC Windchill RCE to KEV as Webshells Land on PLM Servers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-12569 is a CVSS 10.0 deserialization bug in Windchill and FlexPLM, and CISA confirmed active exploitation by adding it to the KEV catalog on June 25.
item.content:encoded:
A perfect-10 remote code execution bug in PTC's Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management suites is being exploited in the wild, and CISA added CVE-2026-12569 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 25. Federal agencies now have a hard deadline to patch, and everyone else should treat that date as their own.

The flaw is an unsafe deserialization of untrusted data, the kind of bug that turns a web request into arbitrary code on the server. No authentication is required. PTC rates it CVSS 10.0, Germany's BSI issued its own critical warning, and the affected footprint includes Windchill's PDMLink module and FlexPLM, the systems that hold a manufacturer's CAD files, bills of materials, and product specs.

What makes this one worth your attention is who runs Windchill. It's the engineering backbone for aerospace, automotive, industrial, and defense suppliers. A webshell on a PLM server isn't a nuisance, it's a window into the design data of whatever the company makes.

And webshells are exactly what's showing up. PTC's advisory describes attackers naming their webshells with 16 lowercase hex characters, so defenders should hunt for any POST request to a path matching /Windchill/login/[16 hex chars].jsp. The intruders also send a custom HTTP header, X-windchill-req, which has no legitimate use in the product. PTC first published indicators on June 18 and has since added more, which tells you the activity is ongoing rather than a single burst.

If you run Windchill or FlexPLM, the order of operations is straightforward. Apply PTC's patch, then go looking for the IOCs, because a patch closes the door but doesn't evict anyone already inside. Check your logs for those JSP paths and the X-windchill-req header going back at least to mid-June, and assume any internet-facing instance was a target.

PLM platforms rarely make the security headlines that VPNs and firewalls do, which is part of why they're attractive. They sit deep in the network, they're trusted, and they're often patched on a sleepy enterprise-software cadence. A CVSS 10 with confirmed exploitation should reset that cadence.

item.title: Three Perfect-10 UniFi OS Bugs Chain to Root, Now Exploited in the Wild
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-34908, -34909, and -34910 to the KEV catalog on June 23 after researchers caught live attacks against Ubiquiti's UniFi OS devices.
item.content:encoded:
Ubiquiti gear is everywhere, from home labs to small-business racks to the network closets of companies that should know better, and three CVSS 10 flaws in UniFi OS just moved from theoretical to actively exploited. CISA added all three to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 23.

The three bugs work as a chain. CVE-2026-34908 is an improper access control issue that lets a remote attacker make unauthorized changes to a device. CVE-2026-34909 is a path traversal flaw for reaching and tampering with files on the underlying OS, including the ones tied to local accounts. CVE-2026-34910 is an input validation weakness that allows command injection over the network. Stitch them together and an unauthenticated attacker gets to root.

The blast radius is the whole UniFi family. Cloud Gateways, Network controllers, Protect NVRs, Access hubs, and Talk appliances all run UniFi OS, so a single unpatched box can hand over the keys to camera feeds, door controls, and the network itself.

Ubiquiti shipped fixes on May 21 in Security Advisory Bulletin 064. Roughly a month later, exploitation caught up. Researchers at PwnDefend reported live attacks landing within days of the advisory, and honeypots are seeing opportunistic probes, which is the usual pattern once a perfect-10 with a public advisory is sitting unpatched on the open internet.

Patch now if you haven't. Then ask the harder question: why is the management interface reachable from the internet at all? UniFi consoles should sit behind a VPN or Ubiquiti's own remote access, not exposed on a public IP. The patch fixes these three CVEs. It does nothing for the next one.

item.title: Mandiant: Cisco SD-WAN Zero-Day Was Exploited Months Before the Patch
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers abused CVE-2026-20245 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager as a zero-day for months, planting a rogue root account before Cisco shipped a fix on June 12.
item.content:encoded:
An attacker uploaded a file called evil_tenant.csv to a Cisco SD-WAN Manager, escalated to root, and created a hidden account named 'troot' with full shell access. Then they did it months before Cisco knew the bug existed.

That's the picture Mandiant painted this week in its analysis of CVE-2026-20245, a flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN that the company patched on June 12. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and lets an authenticated local attacker run arbitrary commands with elevated privileges by feeding the system a malicious CSV file the software fails to validate properly.

The 7.8 rating undersells the operational damage. Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, formerly vManage, is the brain of the network: it pushes policy and config to the SD-WAN Controllers and Validators that steer traffic across an organization's sites. Root on that box is root on the network's control plane.

Mandiant tracked two distinct windows of activity, one running from late 2025 into January 2026 and another in March. In both, the attacker first changed the default admin credentials, then exploited the CSV-parsing flaw to escalate and drop the 'troot' account. That tradecraft, plus the patience to sit on a zero-day for months, points to an actor with a specific objective rather than a smash-and-grab crew.

The uncomfortable part is the timeline. A bug rated medium-high on the CVSS scale was a working zero-day in someone's toolkit for the better part of half a year, against appliances that sit at the center of enterprise networks. If you run Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, patching is step one. Step two is going through your admin accounts and config-change logs for anything you don't recognize, because the fix doesn't remove a user the attacker already created.

item.title: OpenAI's First Chip Is Here: Jalapeño, Built by Broadcom, Aimed at Nvidia
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI and Broadcom revealed Jalapeño, a custom inference ASIC OpenAI says it designed to serve its own models, with first deployment targeted for late 2026.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI now has its own silicon. On June 24 the company and Broadcom unveiled Jalapeño, a custom accelerator built specifically to run inference for OpenAI's models, and the first chip in what the two say will be a multi-generation hardware program.

Inference is the part of the AI business that never stops costing money. Training a model is a one-time spend; serving it to hundreds of millions of ChatGPT users is a bill that arrives every second of every day, most of it paid to Nvidia. A chip designed around OpenAI's own serving patterns is a direct attempt to take that line item in-house.

The technical claims are aggressive. Jalapeño is a reticle-sized ASIC fabricated on a 3-nanometer process, and OpenAI says it went from initial design to manufacturing tape-out in nine months, which the companies call the fastest advanced-ASIC cycle yet. OpenAI also says it used its own models to speed up the design work, and that early engineering samples are already running real workloads in the lab, including a GPT-5.3 Codex variant, at production frequency and power.

OpenAI claims performance per watt 'substantially better' than current state-of-the-art parts. Treat that the way you'd treat any first-silicon benchmark from the team that built it: the number that matters is the one an independent lab measures on a shipping chip, not the one in the launch post.

The structure of the deal is as interesting as the chip. Broadcom handles the silicon implementation and networking, Celestica builds the boards, racks, and systems, and OpenAI gets to point its enormous inference demand at hardware it controls. The companies are targeting initial deployment by the end of 2026, scaling toward gigawatt-class data centers in the years after.

Custom inference chips are not a new idea. Google has run TPUs for a decade, Amazon has Trainium and Inferentia, and Microsoft has its own Maia parts. What's new is OpenAI, the single largest buyer of Nvidia compute on the planet, deciding it would rather build than keep renting. If Jalapeño hits even most of its targets, that's the more consequential story than any benchmark.

item.title: Quantum Computing Inc. Buys a Real Fab in $73M NHanced Deal
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: QCi closed its $73.1 million acquisition of NHanced Semiconductors on June 23, adding chip packaging and fabrication to a company long criticized for thin revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum Computing Inc. closed a $73.1 million acquisition of NHanced Semiconductors on June 23, picking up something the company has been accused of lacking for years: an actual manufacturing operation.

NHanced brings semiconductor and nanophotonics fabrication, advanced packaging expertise, and a team of engineers who build things. QCi frames the deal as its move from research and prototyping toward scalable commercial production, which is a polite way of saying the company would like to ship products instead of press releases.

That framing matters because QCi sits in the most hype-saturated corner of the market. Quantum-computing stocks have ridden waves of enthusiasm that rarely line up with shipped, revenue-generating hardware, and QCi in particular has drawn skeptics who question how much of its valuation rests on real technology versus narrative. Buying a fab with packaging capability is a harder thing to wave away than a roadmap slide.

It's also not a magic fix. Owning a fabrication and packaging operation lowers QCi's dependence on outside foundries and gives it control over how its photonic chips get built, but integration is where these deals usually stall. The test isn't the press release on closing day. It's whether NHanced's lines are turning out QCi parts that customers pay for a year from now.

For anyone watching the broader quantum buildout, the interesting signal is the direction. Several quantum firms have spent 2026 acquiring fabrication and packaging capability rather than licensing it, which suggests the field is grinding toward the unglamorous manufacturing problems that decide whether any of this becomes a product.

item.title: GPT-5 Pro Cracked a T-Cell Puzzle That Stumped a Lab for Three Years
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Immunologist Derya Unutmaz says GPT-5 Pro produced a mechanistic answer to a question his lab had chased since 2022, and OpenAI is leaning hard on the story.
item.content:encoded:
An immunologist fed three years of stuck data into GPT-5 Pro and got back an explanation his entire lab had missed. That's the claim Derya Unutmaz, a researcher at The Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine, made this week, and OpenAI put it front and center on June 24.

The puzzle was a real one in T-cell biology: how does glucose metabolism shape the way T cells develop and specialize? Unutmaz's lab had been circling the question since 2022. According to his account, GPT-5 Pro worked through the dataset and proposed a mechanism, that deoxyglucose blocks the protein IL-2, which would explain why it pushes T cells toward the inflammatory Th17 phenotype.

The detail that makes this harder to dismiss as fancy autocomplete is the second result. Unutmaz says the model also correctly predicted the outcome of unpublished experiments involving CD8+ T cells killing lymphoma cells. If the data wasn't in any training corpus, the model couldn't have simply retrieved the answer, which is the usual deflation for stories like this.

So this is more interesting than the average benchmark win. It's also a single anecdote, told by an enthusiastic user, amplified by the company that sells the product. None of that makes it false. It does mean the honest framing is 'a domain expert used a very strong model to accelerate a hypothesis and then validated it himself,' not 'AI did science.'

That distinction is the whole game right now. A model that generates a sharp, testable hypothesis from messy data is genuinely useful to a working scientist, and Unutmaz is clearly a believer. The work that turns a hypothesis into a result still happens at the bench, run by people who know which answers are worth chasing. Keep both halves of that sentence in view when the next 'AI solved it' headline lands.

item.title: SpaceX Tests Starfall, a Disk-Shaped Capsule to Return Cargo From Orbit
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The uncrewed June 23 demo flew SpaceX's new reentry vehicle, built for in-space manufacturing and rapid cargo return.
item.content:encoded:
It looks like a flying saucer, and that's not a jab at the design. Starfall is a disk: roughly 10 feet across and barely 2.5 feet tall, a shape SpaceX picked on purpose.

The first demonstration flight lifted off June 23 at 6:53 AM EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral, riding a Falcon 9. The capsule was uncrewed, deployed a little after 10 AM ET, and SpaceX reported no anomalies. After demonstrating controlled flight, it was set to splash down in the Pacific.

The vehicle is small and dense. About 3.1 meters in diameter, 0.75 meters tall, around 2,100 kilograms, and able to carry roughly 2,200 pounds of payload. SpaceX is pitching two jobs for it. One is routine, affordable access to microgravity and vacuum for scientific research and in-space manufacturing, the sort of thing companies have wanted cheaply for years. The other is point-to-point delivery of critical cargo through space on fast timelines.

That second use is where the interest gets quieter and more pointed. Cargo delivered anywhere on Earth in under an hour, by way of orbit, is an idea with obvious military logistics appeal, and SpaceX has said very little about the specifics. A few outlets reached for the word "secretive," and the reticence is doing some of that work.

Why the disk shape matters: a wide, flat body sheds reentry heat across a large surface instead of concentrating it on a narrow nose, which can make a returning capsule simpler and cheaper to fly back intact. That's the actual engineering bet here, and a single demo splashdown is a long way from a routine service. But this was the test you run to find out whether the bet holds, and the first one flew clean.

item.title: Chip Stocks Shed $1.3 Trillion as Investors Question AI Spending
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A two-day rout knocked the Nasdaq down 2.2% as the market started asking for returns on the year's $452 billion in AI capital spending.
item.content:encoded:
One point three trillion dollars. That's how much market value semiconductor stocks gave back in the selloff that ran through June 24.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.21% to 25,587 and the S&P 500 fell 1.44%. The pain wasn't evenly spread. Micron tumbled 13% before clawing some of it back, Alphabet slid 6 to 10% across two sessions, and Amazon shed 4%. When memory and the hyperscalers move together like that, it isn't a single bad earnings print. It's sentiment turning.

And the sentiment that turned is specific. For two years the market rewarded any company willing to spend big on AI, no questions asked. That reflex is fading. Combined 2026 capital spending across Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta has now passed $452 billion, and institutional investors are starting to ask the obvious question: where's the revenue that justifies it? Wanting proof of return instead of a roadmap is a healthy instinct. It's also a painful one when the whole sector is priced for the roadmap.

The Federal Reserve added to the mood. Investors who came into the year expecting rate cuts by mid-2026 are recalibrating, because inflation stayed stickier and the economy stayed stronger than the cut-by-summer thesis needed.

The case for calm is that this looks like a valuation reset, not a thesis breaking. Strategists pointed out that S&P 500 tech earnings are still projected to climb more than 22% this year, which is not the profile of a sector falling apart. The real question underneath the selloff isn't whether AI is real. It's whether the spending math works at the multiples these stocks were carrying, and that's a question a few hundred billion in capex makes harder to wave off.

item.title: Qualcomm Buys Modular for $3.9B to Chip at Nvidia's CUDA Lock-In
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Qualcomm's all-stock deal for Modular targets the software moat that keeps AI developers tied to Nvidia hardware, not the silicon itself.
item.content:encoded:
Qualcomm's biggest AI bet this year isn't a chip. It's a compiler.

The company agreed to buy Modular in an all-stock deal worth about $3.92 billion, expected to close in the second half of 2026. Modular is a four-year-old software startup founded by Chris Lattner and Tim Davis, two engineers who met at Google. It builds the Mojo programming language and the MAX inference engine, and the pitch is simple to say and hard to deliver: write your AI code once and run it across chips from different vendors without rewriting it for each one.

That pitch aims directly at the thing that actually protects Nvidia. The hardware is fast, but the real moat is CUDA, the software layer that everything in AI is written against. Once your models and tooling assume CUDA, moving to another vendor's silicon means rewriting the parts that matter, and most teams won't. Break that dependency and a Qualcomm or an AMD chip stops being a science project and starts being a real option.

Worth keeping expectations grounded. The graveyard of CUDA alternatives is not empty, and "portable across any accelerator" has been promised before by people with good engineers and good intentions. The hard part was never the demo. It's getting enough developers to trust the abstraction that the network effect flips. Qualcomm is buying a credible team and a head start, not a finished win.

For Qualcomm the deal fits a larger push past phones, into PCs, automotive, and data center infrastructure. Owning a software layer that doesn't care whose chip runs underneath is a smart place to plant a flag if you're the one trying to sell the other chip. Whether developers show up is the only question that counts, and that answer comes later.

item.title: Google Keeps Losing Its Top AI Researchers to Anthropic and OpenAI
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Two more Gemini researchers are headed to Anthropic, the latest in a run of senior departures that now includes a Nobel laureate and a Transformer co-author.
item.content:encoded:
Jonas Adler and Alexander Pritzel, both of whom worked on Google's Gemini models, are leaving for Anthropic. That's the new item, reported June 24. The pattern around it is the actual story.

In the same stretch of days, two of the biggest names in the field walked out the door. Noam Shazeer, a Gemini co-lead and one of the co-authors of "Attention Is All You Need," the paper that introduced the Transformer, said on June 18 he's going to OpenAI. The next day, John Jumper, who led AlphaFold at DeepMind and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, announced he's joining Anthropic after nearly nine years.

Shazeer's exit stings in a particular way. Google paid a reported $2.7 billion in 2024 to license Character.AI's technology and bring him back into the fold. Two years later he's gone, and the check did not buy lasting loyalty.

Why the one-way traffic? The simplest read is equity. OpenAI and Anthropic are both circling public offerings, and pre-IPO stock is a recruiting lever a mature company can't easily match with refreshed grants. For a senior researcher who already has money, the upside of getting in before the bell rings is the thing that moves them.

The skeptical caveat is real: individual researcher moves are noisy. One departure rarely makes or breaks a model, and Google still ships Gemini at the frontier. But direction matters more than any single name, and right now the direction is consistent. When the people who built your flagship keep choosing the same two competitors, that's not noise, that's a retention problem with a clear address.

Investors noticed. Alphabet slid around 5 to 6 percent on June 22, with analysts tying part of the move to questions about whether Google can hold onto the talent that got it this far.

item.title: CISA Flags Lantronix EDS5000 Bug as Exploited, Patch Due Friday
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A 9.8-severity command injection in Lantronix EDS5000 serial-to-ethernet devices is under active attack, and CISA gave federal agencies until June 26 to fix it.
item.content:encoded:
The attacker doesn't need a valid login. The username they fail with is the payload.

CVE-2025-67038 is a command injection flaw rated 9.8 in the Lantronix EDS5000, and the bug lives somewhere unglamorous: the code that logs a failed authentication. The device's HTTP RPC module takes the username from a failed login attempt and drops it straight into a shell command without sanitizing it first. Feed it a crafted username and you get arbitrary OS commands running as root. No credentials required, because failing the login is the whole point.

What makes this one matter is where these boxes sit. The EDS5000 is a serial-to-ethernet converter, the kind of gear that bridges old industrial and OT equipment to a network so it can be managed remotely. They live in the quiet corners of plant and facility networks, often installed years ago and rarely touched since. Nobody is watching them, and almost nobody patches them on a schedule.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 23, one of four it listed that day. The batch also included max-severity flaws in Ubiquiti UniFi OS, so this wasn't an isolated alert. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were given until June 26 to patch or pull the affected devices.

Lantronix has a fix, version 2.2.0.0R1. The catch is that applying it means someone has to know the device exists, find it, and update firmware on a box that may not have been logged into since it was racked. If you run OT, the move today is to inventory anything Lantronix on your network, get these segmented away from anything that can reach the internet, and schedule the upgrade rather than hoping the device is too obscure to notice. Attackers scanning for 9.8s do not share that assumption.

item.title: Cisco Unified CM Flaw Now Dropping Webshells After Public Exploit
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-20230, an SSRF bug in Cisco Unified Communications Manager, to write files and plant webshells that survive the patch.
item.content:encoded:
The patch came out three weeks ago. The exploitation started last weekend, and it's the kind that doesn't go away once you finally install the fix.

CVE-2026-20230 is a server-side request forgery flaw in Cisco Unified Communications Manager, the system that runs enterprise phone and conferencing infrastructure. Cisco shipped fixes on June 3 and rated it 8.6. The root cause is improper input validation on certain HTTP requests, which lets an attacker abuse the WebDialer component with file:// payloads to write arbitrary files to the underlying OS. From there, the path to root is short.

Threat intelligence firm Defused logged the first real-world attempts over the weekend after exploit details went public. The early activity was reconnaissance: a single IP writing a harmless marker file, /tmp/cve-2026-20230-test.txt, to find vulnerable boxes. That's the polite knock before the door comes off. Honeypots have since seen automated sweeps over Tor dropping webshells, with the observed chain standing up a rogue Apache Axis service to get command execution.

There's one condition that keeps this from being a five-alarm fire for everyone. Exploitation needs the WebDialer service enabled, and it's off by default. So a shop that never turned it on isn't exposed through this path. A shop that did is, and click-to-call WebDialer is common enough in large Cisco voice deployments that plenty of orgs qualify.

Here's the part worth sitting with: patching does not evict an attacker who already wrote a webshell. The fix closes the SSRF door. It does nothing about the persistence someone may have dropped behind it last weekend. If your Unified CM had WebDialer on and you patched late, you patched a house someone may have already keyed.

Concrete next steps. Update to the fixed Unified CM release if you haven't. Check whether WebDialer is actually enabled in your deployment and turn it off where it isn't needed. Then go hunt: look for unexpected files written outside normal paths, any Apache Axis service you didn't deploy, and outbound connections to Tor exit nodes from a voice appliance that has no business talking to them.

item.title: A Refrigerator-Sized Robot Will Try to Save a Falling NASA Telescope
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Katalyst's Link tug launches June 27 on the last-ever Pegasus XL rocket to grab the decaying Swift observatory with robotic arms and boost it back to a safe orbit.
item.content:encoded:
Swift has roughly a 90% chance of falling out of the sky before the end of the year. NASA's plan to stop that involves a refrigerator-sized robot and the last Pegasus rocket that will ever fly.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has been up there since November 2004, hunting gamma-ray bursts and doing it well past its design life. After 21 years, its low orbit has started decaying fast, pushed along by a stretch of heavy solar activity that's thickened the upper atmosphere and added drag. Left alone, it faces an uncontrolled reentry, the kind where nobody gets to choose where the pieces come down.

Enter Katalyst Space Technologies, an Arizona company that won a $30 million task order back in September 2025 with a plan NASA officials politely called technically and programmatically plausible. Their spacecraft is named Link, it's about the size of a refrigerator and roughly twice as heavy, and it carries three robotic arms tipped with LiDAR sensors. The job is to fly up, find Swift, grab a telescope that was never built to be grabbed, and gently push it back toward its original 600-kilometer altitude.

The ride up is its own piece of history. Liftoff is set for June 27 aboard the final Pegasus XL, Northrop Grumman's air-launched booster that gets dropped from a carrier plane before lighting its motor. The drop happens over the equatorial water near Kwajalein Atoll in the Marshall Islands, and the rocket has to thread Link into Swift's orbital plane at a 20.6-degree inclination. After this one, the Pegasus is retired for good.

What makes this worth watching isn't just the save. It's the precedent. Swift was designed in the 1990s with no docking port, no grapple fixture, nothing meant to be serviced by another spacecraft. If a commercial tug can latch onto hardware like that and add years to its life, the math on every aging satellite in orbit changes. The rehearsals have gone well. The real thing is a robot trying to catch a tumbling telescope on the first try, and it gets exactly one.

item.title: Oracle Ships 245 Fixes, and Fusion Middleware Takes the Worst of It
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle's June Critical Security Patch Update covers 243 CVEs across 245 fixes, with Fusion Middleware getting 106 of them, including an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Identity Manager.
item.content:encoded:
Two hundred forty-three CVEs in a single drop. Oracle's June update is the kind of release that quietly ruins a patch team's month, and this one is heavier than most.

The Critical Security Patch Update covers those 243 unique CVEs across 245 fixes, and just under half, 122 of them, carry a critical severity rating. Fusion Middleware ate the largest slice by a wide margin: 106 patches, more than 43% of the entire release. A lot of those are the worst kind, remotely exploitable without any authentication, which is the combination that turns a patch advisory into a weekend.

The one to flag is CVE-2026-21992, an unauthenticated remote code execution bug in Oracle Identity Manager and Oracle Web Services Manager. It lives in the OIM REST WebServices component and hits versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0. An identity-management server is precisely where you don't want a no-credentials RCE, because it sits at the center of who gets access to everything else.

There's a reason this release has urgency behind it rather than the usual quarterly shrug. The same cycle addresses CVE-2026-35273, a PeopleSoft flaw that Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant confirmed was already exploited in the wild as a zero-day by the extortion crew ShinyHunters, tracked as UNC6240. That campaign hit more than 100 organizations, with the bulk of the damage in higher education. When an attacker is already through the door on one Oracle product, the rest of the patch list stops looking optional.

Oracle moved to a monthly security cadence earlier this year, and the volume shows what that actually means in practice: more frequent releases that are still enormous. Prioritize the unauthenticated remote bugs first, Identity Manager included, and don't let the sheer length of the list become an excuse to defer the handful that an attacker can reach from the open internet.

item.title: WhatsApp Campaign Pushes VBScript That Installs ManageEngine RMM
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Kaspersky says an unattributed actor is hijacking WhatsApp accounts to send fake invoice VBS files that quietly install legitimate remote-management software on victims' machines.
item.content:encoded:
The attachment looks like an invoice. Open it, and a script quietly turns your own machine into something someone else can log into whenever they want.

Kaspersky's Securelist team documented an active campaign this month spreading malicious VBScript files through WhatsApp direct messages. The attackers compromise real WhatsApp accounts and use them to send the files, which arrive dressed up as business and financial documents from someone the recipient may actually know. Victims are spread across Malaysia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Singapore, the UK, Spain, Taiwan, Australia, Russia, and Vietnam, with Malaysia taking the heaviest share.

Run the script and it kicks off a multi-stage chain. One stage tries to weaken Windows User Account Control. Another pulls down a ZIP archive containing the installer for a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, ManageEngine's RMM, and sets it up on the host. There's no exotic malware here and that's the point. The attacker installs a real admin tool that endpoint products are inclined to trust, then uses it for hands-on access. It's the same living-off-trusted-software pattern that has made RMM abuse one of the harder intrusions to spot.

Attribution is thin and Kaspersky is careful about it. The campaign isn't tied to a named group. The one thread investigators pulled is an infrastructure overlap, the IP 202.61.160.201, which has shown up in prior activity linked to Gh0st RAT and ValleyRAT, both associated with Chinese-speaking operators. That's a lead, not a conclusion, and it's worth keeping in that lane.

The defensive read is simple and slightly old-fashioned. A document arriving over WhatsApp is still a document from the internet, and a .vbs file has no business being one. Block script execution where you can, watch for RMM tools appearing on machines that never had them, and treat an unexpected ManageEngine install on an endpoint as an incident rather than an IT mystery.

item.title: Squidbleed: A 29-Year-Old Squid Proxy Bug Leaks Cleartext Traffic
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A heap over-read in Squid's FTP gateway, tracked as CVE-2026-47729, can leak other users' HTTP headers, cookies, and session tokens to anyone who can make the proxy fetch a malicious directory listing.
item.content:encoded:
The bug shipped in January 1997. It survived three decades of releases, code reviews, and independent security audits, and nobody noticed until this month.

Researchers are calling it Squidbleed, CVE-2026-47729, and the comparison to Heartbleed is earned. It's a heap buffer over-read in Squid Proxy's FTP gateway. When an attacker's FTP server sends a directory listing line that ends right after the timestamp, a strchr call walks past the buffer and treats the terminating null as part of the search. The result is that raw heap memory gets handed back to whoever asked, and that memory can contain other users' HTTP Authorization headers, cookies, and live session tokens.

Here's who should care. The damage is worst in shared proxy setups, which is to say corporate networks, schools, and public Wi-Fi, anywhere a crowd of people share one Squid instance. Most traffic is HTTPS, which the proxy passes through as an opaque CONNECT tunnel and never sees, so the exposure is really cleartext HTTP and any place the proxy terminates TLS. The attacker also needs the proxy to reach an FTP server they control on port 21. That's a real constraint, but in a lot of default corporate egress, outbound FTP is exactly the kind of thing nobody got around to blocking.

The patch story got messy fast. Early reporting said Squid 7.6 carried the fix. It doesn't. Maintainer Amos Jeffries posted a correction confirming the real CVE-2026-47729 patch is slated for 7.7, which means anyone who upgraded to 7.6 thinking they were covered is not. If you moved to 7.6 on that assumption, you have homework.

There's a cleaner fix available right now, and it costs nothing. Disable FTP gateway support. Every major browser dropped native FTP years ago, so legitimate FTP traffic through a corporate or campus proxy in 2026 is close to nonexistent, and turning the feature off removes this entire bug class instead of just this one CVE. Do that today and patch to 7.7 when it lands.

item.title: OpenAI Wants Its AI to Patch Open Source, Not Just Find the Bugs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI expanded its Daybreak program on June 22 with Patch the Planet, a Codex Security plugin, a vendor partner program, and the full release of GPT-5.5-Cyber scoring 85.6% on CyberGym.
item.content:encoded:
Finding bugs is the easy part now. The harder, more thankless work is writing the fix and convincing an overworked open-source maintainer to merge it. That's the gap OpenAI is aiming at with the expanded version of its Daybreak cybersecurity program.

The centerpiece is Patch the Planet, an initiative built with Trail of Bits and run alongside HackerOne and Calif. The idea is to fund expert researchers, hand them Codex Security and OpenAI's models, and point them straight at the maintainers of the projects everything else depends on. More than 30 projects have signed up so far, with early names including cURL, the Go project, Python, Sigstore, and pyca/cryptography. If you've ever traced a CVE down to a library maintained by one exhausted volunteer, you understand why this is where the leverage actually is.

OpenAI also pushed GPT-5.5-Cyber to a full release, replacing a preview that had been gated to permissive use. The company put its CyberGym score at 85.6%, up from 81.8% for the standard GPT-5.5. Worth knowing what that number is and isn't: CyberGym measures how well a model reproduces and exploits known vulnerability classes in a controlled benchmark. A high score says the model is good at the kind of bug-hunting the benchmark contains. It does not say the model is safe to wire into your pipeline, and it definitely doesn't capture the messy part, which is everything that happens after a finding lands in a real repo.

There's a commercial layer too. The new Daybreak Cyber Partner Program lets vendors fold GPT-5.5 with Trusted Access into the products they sell, with Accenture, Cisco, CrowdStrike, IBM, Okta, Palo Alto Networks, and Wiz as launch partners. That's most of the enterprise security shelf signing on at once.

The timing is hard to ignore. The same day this shipped, the Five Eyes agencies named GPT-5.5-Cyber as an example of a model lowering the barrier to offensive hacking. OpenAI's whole framing is that defenders should get there first, and Patch the Planet is the most concrete version of that argument anyone has put real money behind. The open question is the one no benchmark answers: whether AI that's this good at finding and fixing bugs helps the maintainers more than it helps the people targeting them.

If you maintain something on that list of 30-plus projects, the practical move is to read the patches these researchers send as carefully as you'd read any drive-by pull request. A good patch from a good tool is still a patch you own once you merge it.

item.title: Five Eyes Warns AI Will Supercharge Hacking in Months, Not Years
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The cyber agencies of the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand issued a rare joint warning that frontier models like GPT-5.5-Cyber and Claude Mythos will reshape offensive hacking on a timeline measured in months.
item.content:encoded:
Months, not years. That's the timeline the Five Eyes intelligence agencies put on AI rewriting offensive hacking, in a joint briefing that landed Monday and left very little room to argue.

The cyber chiefs of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand don't issue joint statements often, and they almost never name vendor products when they do. This one did. The brief says frontier models are expected to exceed current industry expectations and transform both offensive and defensive cyber operations, and it puts the window at months rather than years.

The specifics are what make it land. The agencies pointed at OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber and Anthropic's Mythos by name as examples of models already lowering the technical barrier to attacks. They flagged conversational models being used to write phishing at industrial scale, with automated systems scraping public social profiles to produce flawless, targeted lures that don't trip the usual reader's instinct that something is off. None of that is theoretical. It's a description of what's already shipping.

There's an awkward overlap worth saying out loud. The warning went out the same day OpenAI publicly expanded the very program built around GPT-5.5-Cyber, the model the Five Eyes just held up as a risk. The official answer to AI-powered offense is AI-powered defense, and the brief leans on that: use the models to find weaknesses sooner and respond faster. That's a real strategy. It's also the same strategy that gives the offense its tooling, so calling it a clean fix is generous.

For anyone running a security program, the practical takeaways are unglamorous and correct. The agencies told leaders to actually assess their own readiness, fund the basics before chasing AI defense products, give their security leads real authority instead of a title, and assume the phishing they see next quarter will be better written than the phishing they caught last quarter.

The honest read here is that the alliance is trying to move budgets before the curve does. Whether that works depends on whether boards treat a joint Five Eyes brief as a fire alarm or as more noise from people who are paid to worry.

item.title: New Prinz Eugen Ransomware Skips the Note and Goes for Your Newest Files
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A Go-based encryptor spotted this month encrypts recently modified files first and drops no ransom note, keeping the extortion off the victim's machine and out of automated detection.
item.content:encoded:
Most ransomware wants you to know it's there. Prinz Eugen doesn't leave a note.

The new strain, detailed this week, is a Go-based encryptor with two deliberate quirks. First, it goes after the most recently modified files before anything else, and when files share a timestamp it works through them alphabetically. That's not laziness, it's targeting: the files you touched today are the ones you actually need, so encrypting them first maximizes the pain per minute the malware is running.

Second, and more telling, the encryptor has no code to drop a ransom note or change the desktop wallpaper. None. That's a choice organized crews make on purpose. Keeping the demand off the victim's machine cuts the forensic trail and means automated tooling watching for the classic README-HOW-TO-DECRYPT.txt never fires. The extortion happens out of band instead, over email, phone, or a dark-web portal, where it's harder to catch and harder to study.

The operators are hands-on. Initial access looks like stolen RDP credentials, after which a human logs in, leans on legitimate remote monitoring and management tools and other living-off-the-land tricks to move around, then manually runs the payload, a file named servertool.exe. There's no spray-and-pray here. Someone is at the keyboard.

It's early. Researchers have tied at least five organizations to Prinz Eugen so far, and in one reported case the attacker asked for a single bitcoin and was turned down. Small numbers, but the tradecraft is mature, and the no-note approach suggests people who've run this kind of operation before.

The defensive takeaways are the boring ones that keep mattering: lock down RDP behind MFA or a VPN, watch for RMM tools showing up where they don't belong, and keep offline backups that an encryptor running at keyboard speed can't reach. If your alerting leans on spotting a ransom note, this is a reminder that the note is optional and the encryption isn't.

item.title: US Hands SandboxAQ $500M to Find Replacements for Chipmaking's Worst Chemicals
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The CHIPS R&D award funds an AI-driven hunt for PFAS-free process chemicals, rare-earth-free magnets, and other materials the US currently sources from abroad, and the government takes an equity stake in return.
item.content:encoded:
The chips in your phone, your car, and the data center training your favorite model all depend on a class of chemicals nobody has figured out how to replace at scale. The US Department of Commerce is now betting half a billion dollars that an AI company can fix that.

On June 17, SandboxAQ signed a definitive agreement with Commerce's CHIPS R&D office for a $500 million award. The money targets a specific anxiety: the materials and chemistries that semiconductor manufacturing can't run without are largely controlled by foreign suppliers, and a tariff dispute or an export ban could choke domestic fabs that otherwise look self-sufficient on paper.

The work splits into four buckets. The headline one is PFAS, the "forever chemicals" that show up across chip fabrication as heat-transfer fluids, lubricants, insulating coatings, and surface treatments. They're under regulatory pressure for good environmental reasons, and there's no compliant substitute available in volume today. The other three are catalysts, rare-earth-free magnets, and battery systems. SandboxAQ plans to run all of it through its AI materials-discovery platform, which is the part that earned it the Nvidia backing it likes to mention.

Worth slowing down on one detail: the government is taking an equity stake in SandboxAQ as part of this deal. CHIPS money started life as grants. Increasingly it comes with the public buying a piece of the company. Whether that's prudent stewardship of taxpayer dollars or an awkward new role for the state depends on your politics, but it's a real shift in how this program operates, and it's worth watching as more awards land.

The honest caveat is that this is research funding, not a product.
